learning.title: A column default and a real value sharing one name makes them indistinguishable forever
learning.trigger: Adding a discriminator column with a default; writing a conflict clause that decides something from that value; or repairing rows that predate a column.
learning.rule: `origin_kind` was added with `default 'authored'`, so after 0175 the value meant both "this row predates the column" and "a person wrote this". The install upsert then repaired legacy rows with `where origin_kind = 'authored' and slug like 'preset:%'`, which is a predicate that cannot distinguish the two cases: a workflow a person authored under a `preset:` slug was silently rewritten to `catalog` with the catalog's key and revision, and the only record of its real origin was gone.

The blast radius is worth naming precisely, because it decides how loudly to object. No authorization was bypassed and no row was deleted — the damage was false provenance in the column that IS the deliverable, which is exactly the failure the column was added to prevent.

A one-time repair and a per-write repair are different mechanisms with different justifications. `DO NOTHING` plus a data migration keyed to the schema migration says "rows from before the column get fixed once, and the write path never guesses"; an upsert that repairs says "the write path guesses every time". Where the repo already has a data-migration mechanism, using it is not extra ceremony, it is the thing that lets the write path stay honest.

verification.requirement: When a discriminator has a default, state whether that default is also a legitimate value, and if it is, the repair must key on something other than the default — a data migration, a nullable-free backfill, or an explicit marker. Prove the write path cannot rewrite a legitimate value with a test that sets the ambiguous value and performs the real write.
